quote: We shall not use the squared-error rule. Ordinary statisticians take the squared error of everything in sight, but not Bayesian statisticians.
content: The Brier score is a strictly proper scoring rule and Bayesian forecasters use it constantly; the Good Judgment Project scored its superforecasters with it, and the meteorological literature that invented the calibration–discrimination distinction the essay is about to present was built on it. The essay’s derivation of the logarithmic score from the additivity requirement is sound (with additivity over sequential predictions, the score must be a multiple of log P), and the log score’s distinctive property is that it is the unique local proper score, depending only on the probability assigned to what happened (Bernardo (1979)). That is a reason to prefer it for some purposes and a reason to avoid it for others, since it is unbounded and a single zero is fatal, as the essay’s own Bayesianity parable notes. The choice among proper scoring rules is a choice about which errors to penalize (Gneiting & Raftery (2007)); the sneer at statisticians presents a decision as a tribal marker.

quote: If you say “98% probable” a thousand times, and you are surprised only five times, we still ding you for poor calibration. You’re allocating too much probability mass to the possibility that you’re wrong.
content: The distinction between calibration and discrimination that follows has a name and an exact form: Murphy’s decomposition of the Brier score into reliability (calibration), resolution (discrimination) and uncertainty (Murphy (1973)), in which the essay’s claims, that calibration can be repaired by a monotone transform of the forecasts while resolution cannot, are theorems. The essay cites Yates for the qualitative point and presents the structure as its own; it is the standard framework of forecast verification and has been since the 1970s. The point is worth making because the essay’s title promises a technical explanation, and the technical explanation of what the essay is describing is Murphy’s, with the algebra.

quote: Nineteenth century evolutionary theory was wholly semitechnical, without a scrap of quantitative modeling. Not even Mendel’s experiments with peas were then known.
content: Mendel published in 1866 and was ignored, which is not the same as unknown; and the nineteenth century had a quantitative evolutionary tradition that the sentence erases. Galton’s regression to the mean (1877, 1886) and correlation (1888) were invented to model heredity; Pearson and Weldon founded biometry in the 1890s to measure selection in natural populations, and Weldon’s crab studies were quantitative tests of Darwinian selection; Darwin’s own Origin contains the elephant calculation of geometric increase and the 300-million-year estimate for the denudation of the Weald, which he withdrew under criticism. The Kelvin story is also less clean than “history records who won”: Darwin took the age-of-the-Earth objection seriously enough to shift toward faster, more Lamarckian mechanisms in later editions, and the resolution came from radioactivity, that is, from physics correcting physics (Burchfield, Lord Kelvin and the Age of the Earth, 1975). The essay’s moral, that a semitechnical theory can deserve credence against a technical one, is sound; its example was less semitechnical than it says, and the technical opponent lost to a technical correction rather than to a mountain of vague evidence.

quote: Observations of neutron stars confirm the predictions of General Relativity to within one part in a hundred trillion (1014).
content: The number confuses the precision of a measurement with the precision of a test. Pulsar timing determines a rotation period to a part in 1014 or better; the test of general relativity that the timing supports, the orbital decay of the Hulse–Taylor binary from gravitational radiation, agrees with the theory to about 0.2% (Weisberg and Taylor, 2005), and the most precise tests of the theory anywhere are at the level of a few parts in 105 (the Cassini Shapiro-delay measurement, Bertotti, Iess & Tortora (2003)) and, for the double pulsar, about a part in 104 on the best parameter (Kramer et al. (2021)). The essay has overstated the confirmation of its paradigm technical theory by nine orders of magnitude, in a passage whose subject is what it means to be technical. The comparison with evolutionary theory the essay draws next survives with the correct figure, since a part in 105 is still precise; the figure given is not one that any experiment has reached.

quote: Phlogiston was the eighteenth century’s answer to the Elemental Fire of the Greek alchemists. You couldn’t use phlogiston theory to predict the outcome of a chemical transformation—first you looked at the result, then you used phlogiston to explain it. Phlogiston theory was infinitely flexible; a disguised hypothesis of zero knowledge.
content: By the annotator’s count this is the ninth appearance of phlogiston in the book as the type of the empty theory, and it is as wrong here as in Book I. Phlogiston theory predicted that a metal’s calx heated with charcoal would yield the metal (reduction by transfer of phlogiston), that combustion in a sealed vessel would stop when the air was saturated (“phlogisticated”), that metals share a common principle that could be transferred between them, and that the products of combustion of different substances would show systematic relationships; these predictions were made, tested and largely confirmed, which is why the theory organized chemistry for a century and why Priestley, its best experimentalist, isolated oxygen while working within it. Its failure was the weight gain on calcination, which it accommodated badly and Lavoisier explained. That is the history of a theory with content that was superseded, the ordinary case, and the book’s repeated use of it as the paradigm of a theory with no content is a fable that Chang’s Is Water H2O? (2012) and Kuhn’s treatment of the Chemical Revolution had corrected before the essay was reprinted. A book about technical explanation should find a technical example of an empty theory.

quote: But how sad is an algorithm if you can increase its performance by injecting entropy into intermediate processing stages? The algorithm must be so deranged that some of its work goes into concentrating probability mass away from good solutions. If injecting randomness results in a reliable improvement, then some aspect of the algorithm must do reliably worse than random. Only in AI would people devise algorithms literally dumber than a bag of bricks, boost the results slightly back toward ignorance, and then argue for the healing power of noise.
content: The methods that produced the systems the author later reorganized his institute around are built on injected randomness at every stage. Stochastic gradient descent, whose noise is what lets it escape saddle points and find flat minima that generalize (Ge, Huang, Jin and Yuan, “Escaping from Saddle Points,” COLT 2015; Keskar et al., 2017, on the generalization gap); dropout, which randomly deletes units during training and was one of the decisive regularizers of the deep-learning era (Srivastava et al. (2014)); random data augmentation; randomized initialization; sampling at inference. Outside neural networks, simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983)), Markov-chain Monte Carlo, randomized primality testing and hashing are algorithms whose randomness is the mechanism, with theorems about why. None of these is “dumber than a bag of bricks” being nudged back toward ignorance; in each, noise is a search strategy in a landscape where deterministic descent gets stuck, and the improvement is provable. Book I’s annotations found the same error in Lawful Uncertainty, on probability matching. The essay’s thermodynamic intuition, that randomness can only cost, is correct for a convex problem with a known answer and wrong for every problem worth an algorithm; the passage is the book’s clearest prediction about how intelligence would be built, and it was falsified by the building.

quote: How would I explain the event of my left arm being replaced by a blue tentacle? The answer is that I wouldn’t. It isn’t going to happen.
content: The essay has just spent several pages defending Darwin’s post-facto explanation of data he had not anticipated as “correct as probability theory,” and here it says that an event one did not anticipate cannot be explained. The two cannot both hold. Explanation of unanticipated events is most of what science does: the perturbation of Uranus, which the essay praises; the K–T iridium layer; every forensic inference; every diagnosis. The Bayesian statement is that a surprising event is evidence for whichever hypotheses assign it higher likelihood, weighted by their priors, and that after the tentacle one’s posterior over “hallucination, prank, prosthetic, dream” is not zero and one of them wins; the low prior of “webcomic witchcraft” does not stop the update, it directs it toward the mundane alternatives, which is the answer the essay gives in its last paragraph and denies in its first. “Let me miss no jot of my bewilderment” is good emotional advice and the wrong epistemology; bewilderment is the signal that the priors need revising, and revising them, after the fact, on the evidence of the tentacle, is what a Bayesian would do. The essay conflates the vice of retrofitting a favoured hypothesis to any data with the ordinary and necessary act of explaining what one has seen, and the difference between the two is the whole subject of the essay.
